# Exercise 5.3 — Decision trees, overfitting and tuning {#sec-decision-trees}

A decision tree classifies a person by asking a sequence of yes-or-no questions:
is glucose above 128? If so, is body mass above 30? Each answer sends the person
down one branch, until they reach a **leaf**, which gives a predicted class and
a probability. Trees are easy to read, and they can model interactions and
non-linear effects without being told to. Their weakness is that a tree can keep
splitting until it has memorised the training rows. In this exercise we fit a
tree, watch it overfit, restrain it by hand, and then let a grid search choose
the restraint for us.

**Theory:** splits, nodes and leaves; tree depth and minimum node size as
hyperparameters; overfitting in trees; grid search with cross-validation; the
test set is used once, at the end.

::: {.callout-note}
## The plots are for looking at
The code for every plot is folded away just above it, in case you are curious,
and all of it is in the code file linked at the top of each tab. You are not
expected to write it yourself.
:::

### Packages and data

```{r}
# Packages for this exercise. If one is missing, remove the # and run this line once:
# install.packages(c("tidyverse", "tidymodels", "rpart.plot"))

library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(rpart.plot)            # to draw a fitted rpart tree

theme_set(theme_bw())          # white background for every plot
options(pillar.sigfig = 3)     # show three significant figures in tables
```

The same 750 people and split as Exercise 5.2, from
[`data/diabetes.csv`](data/diabetes.csv), with the five predictors pregnant,
glucose, mass, pedigree and age (triceps, insulin and blood pressure are left
out because a zero there means "not measured"). The outcome has the levels
`neg` then `pos`.

```{r}
diabetes <- read_csv("data/diabetes.csv") |>
  select(pregnant, glucose, mass, pedigree, age, diabetes) |>
  filter(glucose > 0, mass > 0) |>              # remove the impossible zeros
  mutate(diabetes = factor(diabetes, levels = c("neg", "pos")))

test_rows <- seq(1, nrow(diabetes), by = 5)     # every fifth person is held back
train <- diabetes[-test_rows, ]
test  <- diabetes[test_rows, ]
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 1 — A basic decision tree

The same three pieces as for logistic regression: a model specification (now
`decision_tree()` with the `rpart` engine), a recipe, and a workflow. The
formula `diabetes ~ .` means "use every other column as a predictor".

```{r}
tree_spec_basic <- decision_tree() |>
  set_engine("rpart") |>
  set_mode("classification")

tree_rec <- recipe(diabetes ~ ., data = train)

tree_wf_basic <- workflow() |>
  add_model(tree_spec_basic) |>
  add_recipe(tree_rec)

tree_fit_basic <- tree_wf_basic |>
  fit(data = train)

tree_fit_basic
```

Each line is a node: the split, the number of people who reach it, how many of
them are misclassified, the predicted class and the two class proportions. A
`*` marks a leaf. Drawing it is easier to read. `extract_fit_engine()` takes the
fitted rpart tree out of the workflow:

```{r}
tree_fit_basic |>
  extract_fit_engine() |>
  rpart.plot(extra = 101, roundint = FALSE)
```

Each box shows the predicted class, the number of people without and with
diabetes who reach it, and their share of the training rows. The first split is
on glucose: everything else depends on it.

rpart's defaults stop the tree early: a split is only kept if it improves the
fit by at least 1% (`cost_complexity = 0.01`), which is why this tree has only 6
leaves. To see what a tree does when nothing stops it, switch that rule off with
`cost_complexity = 0` and let any node with at least 2 people be split
(`min_n = 2`). This is what scikit-learn's default tree does, in the Python tab.

```{r}
tree_spec_full <- decision_tree(cost_complexity = 0, min_n = 2) |>
  set_engine("rpart") |>
  set_mode("classification")

tree_fit_full <- workflow() |>
  add_model(tree_spec_full) |>
  add_recipe(tree_rec) |>
  fit(data = train)

tree_full_frame <- extract_fit_engine(tree_fit_full)$frame   # one row per node
sum(tree_full_frame$var == "<leaf>")                          # number of leaves
```

149 leaves for 600 people: too many to draw.

::: {.callout-important}
## Learning points
- A tree splits the data with one yes-or-no question at a time; each leaf gives a predicted class and a probability.
- The first split is on the most useful predictor, here glucose.
- Default settings differ between packages: rpart stops early, scikit-learn grows the tree until the leaves are pure.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 2 — Does a tree that nothing stops overfit?

Predict the training and the test rows with the tree that nothing stopped.
`type = "class"` uses the threshold 0.5 for us:

```{r}
train_preds_full <- predict(tree_fit_full, new_data = train, type = "prob") |>
  bind_cols(predict(tree_fit_full, new_data = train, type = "class")) |>
  bind_cols(train)

test_preds_full <- predict(tree_fit_full, new_data = test, type = "prob") |>
  bind_cols(predict(tree_fit_full, new_data = test, type = "class")) |>
  bind_cols(test)

conf_mat(train_preds_full, truth = diabetes, estimate = .pred_class)
```

On the training rows the tree makes no mistakes at all. The same metric set as
Exercise 5.2, with `pos` as the event (the second level):

```{r}
class_metrics <- metric_set(accuracy, precision, recall, sens, spec)

class_metrics(train_preds_full, truth = diabetes, estimate = .pred_class,
              event_level = "second")
```

Now the test rows:

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
conf_mat(______, truth = diabetes, estimate = .pred_class)

class_metrics(______, truth = diabetes, estimate = .pred_class,
              event_level = "second")
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
conf_mat(test_preds_full, truth = diabetes, estimate = .pred_class)

class_metrics(test_preds_full, truth = diabetes, estimate = .pred_class,
              event_level = "second")
```

Training accuracy 1.000 in both languages; test accuracy 0.673 in R and 0.693 in
Python (the two trees differ in how ties between equally good splits are
broken). The test sensitivity is 0.434 in R and 0.509 in Python: the tree
misses about half of the people with diabetes it has never seen.
:::
:::

Compare the basic rpart tree of Part 1, which its stopping rule had already
restrained:

```{r}
predict(tree_fit_basic, new_data = train, type = "class") |>
  bind_cols(train) |>
  accuracy(truth = diabetes, estimate = .pred_class)
predict(tree_fit_basic, new_data = test, type = "class") |>
  bind_cols(test) |>
  accuracy(truth = diabetes, estimate = .pred_class)
```

Training accuracy 0.780 and test accuracy 0.787: with 6 leaves the basic tree
does not overfit at all.

**Question!** The tree that nothing stopped is perfect on the training rows and
much worse on the test rows. What has it learned that does not carry over to
new people?

::: {.callout-important}
## Learning points
- A tree that is allowed to keep splitting fits the training rows almost perfectly and does worse on the test rows: it overfits.
- The bigger the gap between training and test performance, the more the model has memorised.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 3 — Restraining the tree by hand

A tree has **hyperparameters**: settings chosen before fitting that control how
complex it can become. In tidymodels:

- `tree_depth`: the maximum number of questions from the root to a leaf;
- `min_n`: the minimum number of people a node must hold before it may be split;
- `cost_complexity`: how much a split must improve the fit to be kept.

Set the first two by hand, to a shallow tree. Keep `cost_complexity = 0`, as for
the tree that nothing stopped in Part 1, so that only the two settings we choose
restrain the tree (the same as in scikit-learn); rpart's 1% rule would
otherwise cut this tree back to a single split.

```{r}
tree_spec_shallow <- decision_tree(cost_complexity = 0,   # no 1% rule, as in Part 1
                                   tree_depth = 3, min_n = 20) |>
  set_engine("rpart") |>
  set_mode("classification")

tree_fit_shallow <- workflow() |>
  add_model(tree_spec_shallow) |>
  add_recipe(tree_rec) |>
  fit(data = train)

tree_fit_shallow |>
  extract_fit_engine() |>
  rpart.plot(extra = 101, roundint = FALSE)
```

The shallow tree is small enough to read as a clinical rule. It has only three
leaves, although it was allowed eight: rpart also drops a split when both of its
sides would predict the same class, because it cannot reduce the number of
mistakes. The scikit-learn tree in the Python tab keeps such splits, but
predicts almost exactly the same classes. Evaluate it on both sets:

```{r}
train_preds_shallow <- predict(tree_fit_shallow, new_data = train, type = "class") |>
  bind_cols(train)
test_preds_shallow <- predict(tree_fit_shallow, new_data = test, type = "class") |>
  bind_cols(test)

class_metrics(train_preds_shallow, truth = diabetes, estimate = .pred_class,
              event_level = "second")
class_metrics(test_preds_shallow, truth = diabetes, estimate = .pred_class,
              event_level = "second")
```

Training accuracy 0.757 in R and 0.760 in Python, test accuracy 0.733 in both
(rpart also refuses to make a leaf with fewer than a third of `min_n` people,
scikit-learn does not, so the two trees differ slightly). Compared with the tree
that nothing stopped, training accuracy has dropped, because the model is
simpler, and test accuracy has risen: the shallow tree generalises better. Try another setting yourself: a tree of depth
5 that may only split nodes holding at least 40 people.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
tree_fit_try <- workflow() |>
  add_model(decision_tree(cost_complexity = 0, tree_depth = ______, min_n = ______) |>
              set_engine("rpart") |>
              set_mode("classification")) |>
  add_recipe(tree_rec) |>
  fit(data = train)

predict(tree_fit_try, new_data = train, type = "class") |>
  bind_cols(train) |>
  accuracy(truth = diabetes, estimate = .pred_class)
predict(tree_fit_try, new_data = test, type = "class") |>
  bind_cols(test) |>
  accuracy(truth = diabetes, estimate = .pred_class)
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
tree_fit_try <- workflow() |>
  add_model(decision_tree(cost_complexity = 0, tree_depth = 5, min_n = 40) |>
              set_engine("rpart") |>
              set_mode("classification")) |>
  add_recipe(tree_rec) |>
  fit(data = train)

predict(tree_fit_try, new_data = train, type = "class") |>
  bind_cols(train) |>
  accuracy(truth = diabetes, estimate = .pred_class)
predict(tree_fit_try, new_data = test, type = "class") |>
  bind_cols(test) |>
  accuracy(truth = diabetes, estimate = .pred_class)
```

R: training accuracy 0.783, test accuracy 0.780. Python: training accuracy
0.785, test accuracy 0.767. Both do better on the test rows than the depth-3
tree.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Learning points
- Hyperparameters such as the maximum depth and the minimum node size control how complex a tree can become.
- A simpler tree fits the training rows less well but can generalise better.
- Trying settings one by one, and judging them on the test rows, does not scale and spends the test set.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 4 — Tuning the hyperparameters with a grid search

Instead of guessing, try a **grid** of values and judge each combination
without touching the test rows. We split the **training** rows into 5 parts
(**folds**); each combination is fitted 5 times, each time on four folds and
evaluated on the fifth, and the 5 results are averaged. This is **5-fold
cross-validation**.

Mark the hyperparameters to be tuned with `tune()`:

```{r}
tree_spec_tune <- decision_tree(cost_complexity = 0, tree_depth = tune(), min_n = tune()) |>
  set_engine("rpart") |>
  set_mode("classification")

tree_wf_cv <- workflow() |>
  add_model(tree_spec_tune) |>
  add_recipe(tree_rec)

tree_grid <- grid_regular(tree_depth(range = c(1L, 10L)),
                          min_n(range = c(2L, 30L)),
                          levels = 5)
tree_grid
```

Five depths times five node sizes: 25 combinations, each fitted on 5 folds.
`vfold_cv()` makes the folds; `strata = diabetes` keeps the share of people with
diabetes the same in every fold. `control_grid(event_level = "second")` tells
the tuning, like every yardstick call on this page, that `pos` is the event.

```{r}
set.seed(123)
folds <- vfold_cv(train, v = 5, strata = diabetes)

tree_res <- tune_grid(
  tree_wf_cv,
  resamples = folds,
  grid      = tree_grid,
  metrics   = metric_set(roc_auc, accuracy),
  control   = control_grid(event_level = "second")
)

show_best(tree_res, metric = "roc_auc", n = 5)
```

```{r}
autoplot(tree_res)
```

A depth of 1 (a single split on glucose) is clearly too simple. When small
nodes may be split (`min_n` 2 or 9) the AUC falls again for deep trees, which
overfit; with `min_n` 23 or 30 deeper trees hold their AUC, because the node
size stops them splitting small groups. Select the best combination, put it
into the workflow, and fit that one tree on all 600 training rows:

```{r}
best_tree <- select_best(tree_res, metric = "roc_auc")
best_tree

final_tree_fit <- finalize_workflow(tree_wf_cv, best_tree) |>
  fit(data = train)

final_tree_fit |>
  extract_fit_engine() |>
  rpart.plot(extra = 101, roundint = FALSE)
```

The tuned tree is shown above. Now, and only now, use the test rows: evaluate
the chosen tree once.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
train_preds_final <- predict(final_tree_fit, new_data = train, type = "prob") |>
  bind_cols(predict(final_tree_fit, new_data = train, type = "class")) |>
  bind_cols(train)
test_preds_final <- predict(final_tree_fit, new_data = ______, type = "prob") |>
  bind_cols(predict(final_tree_fit, new_data = ______, type = "class")) |>
  bind_cols(test)

class_metrics(test_preds_final, truth = diabetes, estimate = .pred_class,
              event_level = "second")
roc_auc(train_preds_final, truth = diabetes, .pred_pos, event_level = "second")
roc_auc(test_preds_final,  truth = diabetes, ______, event_level = "second")
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
train_preds_final <- predict(final_tree_fit, new_data = train, type = "prob") |>
  bind_cols(predict(final_tree_fit, new_data = train, type = "class")) |>
  bind_cols(train)
test_preds_final <- predict(final_tree_fit, new_data = test, type = "prob") |>
  bind_cols(predict(final_tree_fit, new_data = test, type = "class")) |>
  bind_cols(test)

class_metrics(test_preds_final, truth = diabetes, estimate = .pred_class,
              event_level = "second")
roc_auc(train_preds_final, truth = diabetes, .pred_pos, event_level = "second")
roc_auc(test_preds_final,  truth = diabetes, .pred_pos, event_level = "second")
```

R chose `tree_depth` 7 and `min_n` 23 (cross-validated AUC 0.775), a tree with
14 leaves: test accuracy 0.760, sensitivity 0.642, specificity 0.825; AUC 0.854
on the training rows and 0.800 on the test rows. Python chose `max_depth` 5 and
`min_samples_split` 30 (cross-validated AUC 0.767), 15 leaves: test accuracy
0.747, sensitivity 0.585, specificity 0.835; AUC 0.859 on the training rows and
0.782 on the test rows. The gap between training and test is far smaller than
for the tree that nothing stopped, which was perfect on the training rows.
:::
:::

Cross-validation splits the training rows at random, and trees break ties
between equal splits in different ways, so R and Python do not choose the same
tree and their numbers differ.

**Question!** Compare the tuned tree with the basic tree of Part 2. Has the gap
between training and test performance closed? Why must the test rows play no
part in choosing `tree_depth` and `min_n`?

::: {.callout-important}
## Learning points
- A grid search tries every combination of hyperparameter values and judges each by cross-validation on the training rows.
- Hyperparameter tuning is part of training: the test set must never be used to choose hyperparameters, only to evaluate the final model, once.
- Workflows (R) and pipelines (Python) keep the recipe and the model together, so the tuned model is fitted and evaluated exactly as it was tuned.
:::

## Python

[**Download the Python code from this chapter**](code/day5-03-decision-trees.py){download="day5-03-decision-trees.py"} — every cell below, in page order, including the code for every plot, with the blanks left for you to fill in. Open it in Positron beside the page and run it a cell at a time.

### Packages and data

```{python}
# Packages for this exercise. If one is missing, install it once from a terminal
# (in a Jupyter notebook, type %pip instead of pip):
# pip install pandas numpy matplotlib scikit-learn

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, plot_tree
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, precision_score, recall_score
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix, roc_auc_score
```

The same 750 people and split as Exercise 5.2, from
[`data/diabetes.csv`](data/diabetes.csv), with the five predictors pregnant,
glucose, mass, pedigree and age (triceps, insulin and blood pressure are left
out because a zero there means "not measured"). The outcome is 1 for `pos` and
0 for `neg`.

```{python}
diabetes = pd.read_csv("data/diabetes.csv")
diabetes = diabetes[["pregnant", "glucose", "mass", "pedigree", "age", "diabetes"]]
diabetes = diabetes[(diabetes["glucose"] > 0) & (diabetes["mass"] > 0)]   # remove the impossible zeros
diabetes = diabetes.reset_index(drop=True)
diabetes["diabetes"] = (diabetes["diabetes"] == "pos").astype(int)       # 1 = pos, 0 = neg

is_test = diabetes.index % 5 == 0               # every fifth person is held back
train = diabetes[~is_test]
test  = diabetes[is_test]

predictors = ["pregnant", "glucose", "mass", "pedigree", "age"]
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 1 — A basic decision tree

A `DecisionTreeClassifier()` with its default settings, fitted on the five
predictors. `random_state` fixes how ties between equally good splits are
broken, so that the tree is the same every time.

```{python}
tree_basic = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=123)
tree_basic = tree_basic.fit(train[predictors], train["diabetes"])

print("depth: ", tree_basic.get_depth())
print("leaves:", tree_basic.get_n_leaves())
```

The default tree keeps splitting until every leaf is pure: it has grown to a
depth of 18 with 151 leaves for 600 people. Draw the top three levels
(`max_depth=3` only limits the drawing, not the tree):

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(22, 8))
drawn = plot_tree(tree_basic, max_depth=3, feature_names=predictors,
                  class_names=["neg", "pos"], filled=True, fontsize=8, ax=ax)
plt.show()
```

In each box: the split, the Gini impurity (0 for a pure node), the number of
people (`samples`), how many of them are without and with diabetes (`value`),
and the predicted class. The first split is on glucose: everything else depends
on it.

scikit-learn's defaults grow the tree until every leaf is pure. R's rpart stops
early by default (a split is only kept if it improves the fit by at least 1%),
so in the R tab the same data give a much smaller tree.

::: {.callout-important}
## Learning points
- A tree splits the data with one yes-or-no question at a time; each leaf gives a predicted class and a probability.
- The first split is on the most useful predictor, here glucose.
- Default settings differ between packages: rpart stops early, scikit-learn grows the tree until the leaves are pure.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 2 — Does a tree that nothing stops overfit?

Predict the training and the test rows. `predict()` uses the threshold 0.5 for
us:

```{python}
train_preds_basic = train.copy()
train_preds_basic["prob"] = tree_basic.predict_proba(train[predictors])[:, 1]
train_preds_basic["pred_class"] = tree_basic.predict(train[predictors])

test_preds_basic = test.copy()
test_preds_basic["prob"] = tree_basic.predict_proba(test[predictors])[:, 1]
test_preds_basic["pred_class"] = tree_basic.predict(test[predictors])

confusion_matrix(train_preds_basic["diabetes"], train_preds_basic["pred_class"])
```

The same metrics as Exercise 5.2. Remember that `confusion_matrix()` puts the
truth in the rows. On the training rows the tree makes no mistakes at all:

```{python}
truth, predicted = train_preds_basic["diabetes"], train_preds_basic["pred_class"]

print("accuracy:   ", round(accuracy_score(truth, predicted), 3))
print("precision:  ", round(precision_score(truth, predicted), 3))
print("sensitivity:", round(recall_score(truth, predicted), 3))
print("specificity:", round(recall_score(truth, predicted, pos_label=0), 3))
```

Now the test rows:

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
truth, predicted = ______, test_preds_basic["pred_class"]

print(confusion_matrix(truth, predicted))
print("accuracy:   ", round(accuracy_score(truth, predicted), 3))
print("precision:  ", round(precision_score(truth, predicted), 3))
print("sensitivity:", round(recall_score(truth, predicted), 3))
print("specificity:", round(______, 3))
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
truth, predicted = test_preds_basic["diabetes"], test_preds_basic["pred_class"]

print(confusion_matrix(truth, predicted))
print("accuracy:   ", round(accuracy_score(truth, predicted), 3))
print("precision:  ", round(precision_score(truth, predicted), 3))
print("sensitivity:", round(recall_score(truth, predicted), 3))
print("specificity:", round(recall_score(truth, predicted, pos_label=0), 3))
```

Training accuracy 1.000 in both languages; test accuracy 0.673 in R and 0.693 in
Python (the two trees differ in how ties between equally good splits are
broken). The test sensitivity is 0.434 in R and 0.509 in Python: the tree
misses about half of the people with diabetes it has never seen.
:::
:::

**Question!** The tree is perfect on the training rows and much worse on the
test rows. What has it learned that does not carry over to new people?

::: {.callout-important}
## Learning points
- A tree that is allowed to keep splitting fits the training rows almost perfectly and does worse on the test rows: it overfits.
- The bigger the gap between training and test performance, the more the model has memorised.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 3 — Restraining the tree by hand

A tree has **hyperparameters**: settings chosen before fitting that control how
complex it can become. In scikit-learn:

- `max_depth`: the maximum number of questions from the root to a leaf;
- `min_samples_split`: the minimum number of people a node must hold before it
  may be split;
- `ccp_alpha`: how much a split must improve the fit to be kept.

Set the first two by hand, to a shallow tree:

```{python}
tree_shallow = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3, min_samples_split=20, random_state=123)
tree_shallow = tree_shallow.fit(train[predictors], train["diabetes"])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(14, 7))
drawn = plot_tree(tree_shallow, feature_names=predictors,
                  class_names=["neg", "pos"], filled=True, fontsize=9, ax=ax)
plt.show()
```

The shallow tree is small enough to read as a clinical rule. Most of its leaves
predict `neg`; only people with high glucose and a high body mass are predicted
to have diabetes. Evaluate it on both sets:

```{python}
for name, data in [("train", train), ("test", test)]:
    truth = data["diabetes"]
    predicted = tree_shallow.predict(data[predictors])
    print(name,
          "accuracy", round(accuracy_score(truth, predicted), 3),
          "precision", round(precision_score(truth, predicted), 3),
          "sensitivity", round(recall_score(truth, predicted), 3),
          "specificity", round(recall_score(truth, predicted, pos_label=0), 3))
```

Training accuracy 0.757 in R and 0.760 in Python, test accuracy 0.733 in both
(rpart also refuses to make a leaf with fewer than a third of `min_n` people,
scikit-learn does not, so the two trees differ slightly). Compared with the tree
that nothing stopped, training accuracy has dropped, because the model is
simpler, and test accuracy has risen: the shallow tree generalises better. Try another setting yourself: a tree of depth
5 that may only split nodes holding at least 40 people.

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
tree_try = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=______, min_samples_split=______, random_state=123)
tree_try = tree_try.fit(train[predictors], train["diabetes"])

print("train accuracy:", round(accuracy_score(train["diabetes"], tree_try.predict(train[predictors])), 3))
print("test accuracy: ", round(accuracy_score(test["diabetes"], tree_try.predict(test[predictors])), 3))
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
tree_try = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=5, min_samples_split=40, random_state=123)
tree_try = tree_try.fit(train[predictors], train["diabetes"])

print("train accuracy:", round(accuracy_score(train["diabetes"], tree_try.predict(train[predictors])), 3))
print("test accuracy: ", round(accuracy_score(test["diabetes"], tree_try.predict(test[predictors])), 3))
```

R: training accuracy 0.783, test accuracy 0.780. Python: training accuracy
0.785, test accuracy 0.767. Both do better on the test rows than the depth-3
tree.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Learning points
- Hyperparameters such as the maximum depth and the minimum node size control how complex a tree can become.
- A simpler tree fits the training rows less well but can generalise better.
- Trying settings one by one, and judging them on the test rows, does not scale and spends the test set.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 4 — Tuning the hyperparameters with a grid search

Instead of guessing, try a **grid** of values and judge each combination
without touching the test rows. We split the **training** rows into 5 parts
(**folds**); each combination is fitted 5 times, each time on four folds and
evaluated on the fifth, and the 5 results are averaged. This is **5-fold
cross-validation**, and `GridSearchCV()` does all of it.

```{python}
tree_grid = {"max_depth":         [1, 3, 5, 7, 10],
             "min_samples_split": [2, 9, 16, 23, 30]}
```

Five depths times five node sizes: 25 combinations, each fitted on 5 folds.
`cv=5` makes the folds, keeping the share of people with diabetes the same in
every fold; `scoring="roc_auc"` judges each combination by its AUC.

```{python}
tree_search = GridSearchCV(DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=123),
                           param_grid=tree_grid, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc")
tree_search = tree_search.fit(train[predictors], train["diabetes"])

tree_results = pd.DataFrame(tree_search.cv_results_)
tree_results = tree_results[["param_max_depth", "param_min_samples_split",
                             "mean_test_score", "std_test_score"]]
tree_results.sort_values("mean_test_score", ascending=False).head(5).round(3)
```

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for split in tree_grid["min_samples_split"]:
    rows = tree_results[tree_results["param_min_samples_split"] == split]
    ax.plot(rows["param_max_depth"], rows["mean_test_score"], marker="o", label=str(split))
ax.set_xlabel("max_depth")
ax.set_ylabel("Mean cross-validated AUC")
ax.legend(title="min_samples_split")
plt.show()
```

A depth of 1 (a single split on glucose) is clearly too simple, and so are deep
trees that may split small nodes: the AUC falls as the tree gets deeper, unless
`min_samples_split` is large. Select the best combination; `GridSearchCV()` has
already refitted it on all 600 training rows (`refit=True` is the default):

```{python}
print(tree_search.best_params_)
print("cross-validated AUC:", round(tree_search.best_score_, 3))

final_tree = tree_search.best_estimator_
print("leaves:", final_tree.get_n_leaves())
```

Now, and only now, use the test rows: evaluate the chosen tree once.

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
test_prob  = final_tree.predict_proba(test[predictors])[:, 1]
test_class = final_tree.predict(______)
train_prob = final_tree.predict_proba(train[predictors])[:, 1]

print("test accuracy:   ", round(accuracy_score(test["diabetes"], test_class), 3))
print("test sensitivity:", round(recall_score(test["diabetes"], test_class), 3))
print("test specificity:", round(recall_score(test["diabetes"], test_class, pos_label=0), 3))
print("train AUC:", round(roc_auc_score(train["diabetes"], train_prob), 3))
print("test AUC: ", round(roc_auc_score(test["diabetes"], ______), 3))
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
test_prob  = final_tree.predict_proba(test[predictors])[:, 1]
test_class = final_tree.predict(test[predictors])
train_prob = final_tree.predict_proba(train[predictors])[:, 1]

print("test accuracy:   ", round(accuracy_score(test["diabetes"], test_class), 3))
print("test sensitivity:", round(recall_score(test["diabetes"], test_class), 3))
print("test specificity:", round(recall_score(test["diabetes"], test_class, pos_label=0), 3))
print("train AUC:", round(roc_auc_score(train["diabetes"], train_prob), 3))
print("test AUC: ", round(roc_auc_score(test["diabetes"], test_prob), 3))
```

R chose `tree_depth` 7 and `min_n` 23 (cross-validated AUC 0.775), a tree with
14 leaves: test accuracy 0.760, sensitivity 0.642, specificity 0.825; AUC 0.854
on the training rows and 0.800 on the test rows. Python chose `max_depth` 5 and
`min_samples_split` 30 (cross-validated AUC 0.767), 15 leaves: test accuracy
0.747, sensitivity 0.585, specificity 0.835; AUC 0.859 on the training rows and
0.782 on the test rows. The gap between training and test is far smaller than
for the tree that nothing stopped, which was perfect on the training rows.
:::
:::

Cross-validation splits the training rows at random, and trees break ties
between equal splits in different ways, so R and Python do not choose the same
tree and their numbers differ.

**Question!** Compare the tuned tree with the basic tree of Part 2. Has the gap
between training and test performance closed? Why must the test rows play no
part in choosing `tree_depth` and `min_n`?

::: {.callout-important}
## Learning points
- A grid search tries every combination of hyperparameter values and judges each by cross-validation on the training rows.
- Hyperparameter tuning is part of training: the test set must never be used to choose hyperparameters, only to evaluate the final model, once.
- Workflows (R) and pipelines (Python) keep the recipe and the model together, so the tuned model is fitted and evaluated exactly as it was tuned.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::: {.instructor}
**Teaching choice.** The module lead's page used the full Pima data (all eight
predictors, stratified random 70/30 split, `pos` as first level) and tuned with
a single bootstrap resample. This version uses the shared Day 4 split, the five
predictors without hidden missing values, `event_level = "second"`, and 5-fold
cross-validation (`vfold_cv(v = 5, strata = diabetes)`; `cv=5` in Python, which
is stratified), as her own code comment suggested. On this split her default
rpart tree does not overfit (6 leaves, train 0.780, test 0.787), so Part 1 adds
the tree with `cost_complexity = 0` to show the overfitting her page described,
and Parts 3 and 4 keep `cost_complexity = 0` so that R tunes the same two
hyperparameters as Python (`min_n` = `min_samples_split`). Her grid (depth 1 to
10, `min_n` 2 to 30, five levels each) is kept.

**Expected values.** R basic tree (defaults): 6 leaves, first split glucose
< 154.5; train accuracy 0.780, test 0.787. Unstopped tree: R 149 leaves, depth
16; Python 151 leaves, depth 18. Both train accuracy 1.000; test accuracy 0.673
(R) and 0.693 (Python); test sensitivity 0.434 / 0.509, specificity 0.804 /
0.794; R test confusion table predicted neg 78 / 30, pos 19 / 23. Depth 3,
`min_n` 20: R 3 leaves drawn, train 0.757, test 0.733 (sensitivity 0.340,
specificity 0.948); Python 8 leaves, train 0.760, test 0.733. Depth 5, `min_n`
40 (Task 2): R 0.783 / 0.780, Python 0.785 / 0.767. Tuning (`set.seed(123)`):
R best depth 7, `min_n` 23, CV AUC 0.775 (SE 0.018), 14 leaves, test accuracy
0.760, sensitivity 0.642, specificity 0.825, AUC train 0.854, test 0.800.
Python best depth 5, `min_samples_split` 30, CV AUC 0.767, 15 leaves, test
accuracy 0.747, sensitivity 0.585, specificity 0.835, AUC train 0.859, test
0.782. Cross-validation folds and tie-breaking differ between the languages, so
the tuned trees differ.

**Common failures.** (1) Calling `rpart.plot()` without `roundint = FALSE`:
it warns that it cannot retrieve the data. (2) Forgetting `event_level =
"second"`, which swaps sensitivity and specificity. (3) Tuning on `test`, or
finalising before `select_best()`. (4) Expecting the same chosen
hyperparameters as a neighbour who used a different seed: several combinations
lie within one standard error of the best. (5) In Python, reading
`plot_tree(max_depth=3)` as a depth-3 model: it only limits the drawing.

**Timing.** Part 1 fifteen minutes, Part 2 fifteen, Part 3 fifteen, Part 4
twenty-five.
